lesson_title: The Torn Photograph: Proving the Continents Move
hook_text: Africa and South America are two halves of a torn photograph. Here's the proof.
clip_script: Take an old family photograph and tear it in two. Years later the halves surface again — how do you prove they belong together? The torn edges matching is suggestive. But the real proof is the picture: if a face continues across the tear, the argument is finished. The continents are that photograph. The matching edge is the coastline — South America nesting into the curve of West Africa. And the picture runs across the tear. A little freshwater reptile called Mesosaurus, which could never have crossed an ocean, lies in the rocks of the Karoo — and lies again in Brazil. The Cape Fold Mountains run down our coast, stop at the sea, and stand up again in Argentina: same rocks, same age, same folding. Near Barkly West you can touch bedrock scratched by glaciers — an ice sheet, in a hot country — and the scratch directions in Africa, South America, India and Australia all point away from one centre, but only if you push the continents back together first. Wegener showed all this in 1912 and was laughed at anyway, because he could not say what did the pushing.
visual_style: A sepia photograph tearing in two and drifting apart, fossils and mountain ranges glowing as they line up across the tear; glacial scratches swinging into alignment as continents slide home.
mood: Detective story — a century-old case cracked with evidence you can still touch.
pacing: Steady build through the clues, a beat of triumph at the reassembly, wry landing on Wegener's rejection.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to meet the engine Wegener never found.
